hints: Start by writing the dissolving equilibrium for $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(\text{s})$ and remember that pure solids are omitted from equilibrium expressions.
Think about how the 2:1 ratio of $\text{Ag}^+$ to $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ appears as a power, and how units multiply from each concentration term.
walkthrough:
Write the heterogeneous equilibrium**
Picture solid silver carbonate in contact with water: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(\text{s}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(\text{aq})$. For any equilibrium constant you only include species whose concentration can change, so the solid with constant density is left out.

Apply powers from stoichiometry**
Each $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$ gives two $\text{Ag}^+$ ions, so $[\text{Ag}^+]$ is squared. Carbonate appears once, so it is to the power one. That gives $K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+]^2[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$.

Work out the units**
Each concentration has units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Multiplying $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2 \times (\text{mol dm}^{-3})$ gives $\text{mol}^3 \text{dm}^{-9}$.

hints: Let the solubility of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$ be $x$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, then express $[\text{Ag}^+]$ and $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$ in terms of $x$ before substituting into $K_{sp}$.
walkthrough:
Link solubility to ion concentrations**
If $x$ mol of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$ dissolves in $1 \text{ dm}^3$, you get $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = x$ and $[\text{Ag}^+] = 2x$ because of the 2:1 ratio. This factor of 2 is the most common slip, so keep it visible.

Substitute and solve**
$$K_{sp} = (2x)^2(x) = 4x^3 = 6.3 \times 10^{-12}$$
$$x = \sqrt[3]{\frac{6.3 \times 10^{-12}}{4}} = 1.16 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
Then $[\text{Ag}^+] = 2x = 2.33 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

hints: In $0.050$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{AgNO}_3$, the $[\text{Ag}^+]$ is fixed by the added salt and the tiny extra from $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$ can be ignored.
walkthrough:
Use the common ion to suppress solubility**
$\text{AgNO}_3$ is fully dissociated, so $[\text{Ag}^+] \approx 0.050 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. The $K_{sp}$ value is unchanged at the same temperature, only the ion concentrations adjust.

Rearrange $K_{sp}$ for carbonate**
$$6.3 \times 10^{-12} = [0.050]^2[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$$
$$[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = \frac{6.3 \times 10^{-12}}{(0.050)^2} = 2.52 \times 10^{-9} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
Notice how dramatically the solubility is lowered compared with pure water. That is the common ion effect in action.

hints: Recall the Nernst form for a $\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}$ electrode at 298 K: $E = E^{\ominus} + 0.059\log[\text{Ag}^+]$, with $E^{\ominus} = +0.80$ V from the Data Booklet.
Consider why $E$ will be less positive than $E^{\ominus}$ when $[\text{Ag}^+]$ is far below $1.00$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Nernst equation**
For $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}(\text{s})$, lowering $[\text{Ag}^+]$ shifts equilibrium to the left, making reduction less favourable. Quantitatively: $$E = E^{\ominus} + 0.059\log[\text{Ag}^+]$$ with $E^{\ominus} = +0.80$ V.

Insert the saturated concentration**
Use $[\text{Ag}^+] = 2.33 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ from (a)(ii):
$$E = 0.80 + 0.059\log(2.33 \times 10^{-4})$$
$$E = 0.80 - 0.214 = 0.57 \text{ V}$$
The log term is negative because the concentration is less than 1, so $E$ drops below standard.

hints: Apply $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ using the table values for $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})$, $\text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})$ and $\text{AgCl}(\text{s})$.
walkthrough:
Add up entropies correctly**
Dissolving breaks an ordered lattice into mobile hydrated ions, but hydration also orders water. Calculate net change:
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = S^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^+) + S^{\ominus}(\text{Cl}^-) - S^{\ominus}(\text{AgCl})$$
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = 72.7 + 56.5 - 96.2 = +33.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$
The positive sign means increased disorder overall.
Final answer: $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +33.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall the link between feasibility and Gibbs energy: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ with $T = 298$ K.
Check units carefully: $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ while $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is in $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$, so convert one to match the other.
Think about what the sign of your calculated $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ tells you about whether dissolving can happen spontaneously.
walkthrough:
Write the Gibbs equation**
Feasibility at constant $T$ and $p$ is decided by $\Delta G^{\ominus}$. Even with favourable entropy, a large positive $\Delta H$ can dominate: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$

Substitute with consistent units**
$T = 25^{\circ}\text{C} = 298$ K. Convert $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +33.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} = 0.0330 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 65.5 - (298 \times 0.0330)$$
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 65.5 - 9.83 = +55.7 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Interpret the sign**
A large positive $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ means the dissolving process is not spontaneous under standard conditions. The endothermic enthalpy term outweighs the $T\Delta S$ term, so equilibrium lies far to the left and $\text{AgCl}$ remains essentially insoluble.

Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus} = 65.5 - (298 \times 0.033) = +55.7 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus}$ is positive so dissolving is not feasible, hence AgCl is insoluble.
